Oṃ, salutations to the Destroyer of Obstacles.
Śrī Na Ja U Ca.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the greatness of Śuka,
as well as the mutual conversation between Vyāsa and Śuka.
O high-minded one, tell me of that delightful hermitage where that great conversation took place between the father and his son.
Listen attentively, O King, to this conversation of those great-souled ones, which I heard and which was wonderful and hair-raising. (3)
There, in that delightful hermitage, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
in a region renowned throughout the three worlds and inhabited by various sages.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers,
and possessed delightful lakes of various shapes, full of water.
It was strewn with flocks of swans and adorned by groups of cakravāka birds,
which produced sweet, melodious sounds and most delightful "hum" calls.
It was constantly frequented by birds of various forms, by lotuses crowded with swarms of bees, and by Brahmins who were the foremost among sages.
And the sound of the Vedas is heard from those performing the Agnihotra sacrifice;
there, O King, the Blessed One resides in that beautiful hermitage, Āśramapada.
Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, the great sage who is the expounder of the Vedas, had a son named Śuka, a great yogi among high-souled beings. (9)
Having constantly questioned his father, who was learned in all the scriptures,
and having clasped his feet, he spoke these words.
Abandoning passion and hatred, listen to the words spoken by your father:
"In this worldly existence, which is a great ocean of profound delusion, various things have been seen. (11)
Mothers and fathers, as well as thousands of kinsmen, ornaments, deeds, youth, and riches—[all these are transitory]. (12)
Having come and gone through various animal wombs,
I wandered there like a bound beast, wherever I was tethered.
I have reached the human world, this field of action so difficult to attain;
I have obtained that ancient stairway to heaven which leads according to dharma.
Formerly, this was the abode of Truth, frequented by the Gaṇas, and illuminated on all sides by constellations and stars. (15)
There, I enjoyed the most excellent pleasures that I had envisioned;
yet, I have fallen from my good fortune like a planet whose merit has been exhausted.
Among worms, insects, and moths, and among the hundreds of animal wombs—whether born from eggs, born from sweat, born from moisture, or born from a split—(they are reborn). 17.
Likewise, those born from sprouts, those born from moisture, and others born from various wombs—even among hundreds such as lions, tigers, boars, cats, and so forth—[attain this state]. (18)
I was a worm for ten years, a moth for fourteen,
and likewise born from an egg for a hundred years again.
I was a lion for ten years, and a tiger for fifteen;
I was a boar for five years, and I was also a bear for fifteen. (20)
For twenty years I was a mole, and fourteen years a lizard;
for thirty years I was a snake, and thirteen years a jackal. (21)
For seventy years he was an elephant, for ten years a donkey;
for seven years he was a swan, and for ten years a cātaka bird.
For fifteen years I was a vulture, for ten years I was a crow,
and I remained in the state of an immobile being for five hundred years as well.
Thus, while wandering constantly through thousands of births,
O father, even in my state as a bird, I experienced most terrible hunger and thirst.
In the animal realm I was constantly itchy, while in the state of stationary beings I was covered in frost;
in this manner, indeed, thousands of years were experienced by me.
I remember all my births, indeed thousands of them;
recollecting each one individually in detail, I have attained dissolution [into the Self]. (26)
Therefore, seeing again and again the terrible hells and the difficult-to-cross ocean of saṃsāra, I am utterly terrified. (27)
I am pierced by various scriptures and by the messengers of Yama with their most terrible afflictions;
I am terrified of the ocean of saṃsāra, presided over by the five elements. (28)
All this consists of desire; the objects of the five senses are likewise so. Fearing old age and death, what shall I do with this? (29)
Having heard those words of that high-souled Śuka,
the great yogi, his eyes filled with tears, fell from his seat to the ground.
Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the great sage Vedavyāsa, having resorted to a Vaiṣṇava woman, was deluded by affection for his son. (31)
"How is it, my son, that you have abandoned your mother and father, as well as your kinsmen, friends, and well-wishing relatives? (32)
"O my son, you surely desire to depart on your journey;
indeed, I have no need whatsoever for the life of my wife. (33)
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives have been experienced in this cycle of existence; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?
"By me, who am unborn, thousands have been born through that very reality of egoism; even by him a son was born—behold the unfolding of Māyā! (35)
Agastya, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Bhṛgu, and likewise Aṅgiras—they too have fallen under the power of death; therefore, I have no need for life.
Parāśara, the high-souled one, and the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya—even they have fallen under the power of death; therefore, I have no need for life.
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Viśvāmitra—even they have fallen under the power of death; therefore, I have no need for life.
Durvāsas, Lomaharṣa, Śāṇḍilya, and Punarvasu—they too have fallen into the power of death; there is no purpose for my life.
Saumya, Saṃvartaka, and likewise Gārgika and Ātāyana—they too have fallen under the power of death; therefore, I have no need for life.
Even those who possess ten lights, a hundred lights, or a thousand lights, are subject to the power of death; therefore, I have no concern for life.
With arms raised, Mārkaṇḍeya subsisted on air and water;
these and many others have come within the domain of death. (31)
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Rāvaṇa, and likewise Indrajit;
the two Asuras Sunda and Upasunda, and the exceedingly powerful Kālanemi.
Nīla, Jāmbavān, Sugrīva, Gandhamādana, Subāhu, and other monkeys of great splendor were there as well. (33)
The gods and the rākṣasas alike [acknowledge] Kumbhakarṇa as being exceedingly powerful,
as well as Akṣa, Mahodara, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka.
Khara, Śūrpaṇakhā, and all others have fallen under the power of death;
so too has King Duryodhana, as well as Pārtha, Bhīṣma, and Yudhiṣṭhira. (35)
Indra, Dhanada, and likewise Antaka in the world of Yama—such [beings] belong to humans and to sages of purified souls. (36)
The fourfold assembly of living beings among all creatures dies;
know this, O father: everyone will surely go to their destruction. (37)
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, these worlds, both moving and unmoving, have inspired in me a sense of world-weariness; I am now setting out on my departure.
I am terrified of the ocean of saṃsāra and have no doubt that I desire to depart from it. I shall go to that very place where you wish to go.
O son, you have been contemplated by me in vain through hundreds of desires.
And he will be my refuge, for I am bound by the snares of hope.
I am not the son of anyone, nor is there anyone who is my father;
indeed, I have been born thousands of times, and I have begotten [sons] by the thousands.
No person is born by another person; a person does not truly know other persons.
Indeed, it is the self that grieves for a person, and a person grieves for his own self. (43)
"I am indeed your son, born of you; yet by me, thousands of sons have been born from Jāḍyā.
Behold, even a son is born from a son—those who are utterly deluded by Māyā! (44)
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, including gods, asuras, and humans,
is pervaded by the subtle, supreme, and great-souled Lord.
By what color indeed can that which was created by the Blessed One, Hari, the sustainer of the worlds, ever be known through knowledge? || 46 ||
Fearing birth and death again and again in life after life, I am terrified;
yet, O Father, it is not enough that you continue to delude me once more. (47)
Whatever great thought was conceived by me while dwelling in the wombs of rebirth—that hell has been transcended by me, and knowledge, so difficult to attain, has been gained. (48)
Cold, heat, hunger, and thirst are terrible during the dwellings in the womb;
O Father, there is no other fear more painful than dwelling in the womb. (49)
"Because of the fickleness of the senses and because of the seasonal fondling of women, this semen was produced by me; what was done by you in that matter? (50)
I am not the son of anyone, nor have I been born by anyone;
I am bound by my past actions through the instability of the senses.
If, upon the death of the father, the son, or if the father, upon the death of the son, gives up his life, behold the unfolding of Māyā! (52)
If it was not previously taught in the meaning of the Gītā that rebirth does not exist, then how could there be rebirth for one who has perished, O Lord? It does not exist.
"O dear one, even in Bhārata you previously foresaw the future;
though you have become a seer of the three times, why do you grieve like a fool? (54)
Just as one might try to grasp the sky with fists or shatter chaff with grain-husks, so too have you failed to comprehend the meaning of the Gītā within the Bhārata scripture. 55.
Whose mother and whose father are they? Whose kinsmen are they, O Great Sage? It is through delusion and the loss of memory that living beings become bewildered. (56)
I am alone, one without a second; I do not belong to anyone else. I do not see anyone to whom I belong, nor does anyone see me.
Neither a friend nor a relative comes along with one, nor wealth accumulated through effort, nor sons, nor a wife;
at the very moment when a man's life-breaths depart, leaving behind hundreds of dear things, they go forth with only the wealth of the path that is the fruit of one's own karma. (58)
"O wife! O sons! O self! O happiness!
O mother! O brother! Behold how [the world] is deluded by illusion! (59)
Dharma alone is mother and father, O great sage; Dharma is one's kinsman.
Various mothers have been seen, and various kinds of breasts have been sucked. (60)
In this cycle of existence, many fathers have passed away one after another;
thus, through wandering in saṃsāra, I have attained the desired state.
Through the grace of the God of gods, the Great-Souled Lord,
by whom the year was seen and the Creator was worshipped but once.
By him all this has been seen: that the world returns again, for all those traveling together as a single caravan must go there. (63)
If one departs in haste, what lamentation can there be for that?
It is like the gathering of various birds upon a single tree at night. (64)
Just as [rays] go forth in the ten directions at dawn, so too is the gathering of living beings. || 65 ||
"Youth is seized by old age, health is destroyed by diseases, and death devours all beings; why do you speak as if you were a wise man? (66)
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart, even so is the meeting of living beings. (67)

Some desire to dwell even in the hells rather than dwelling within the region of a womb; for hell is distinguished as better than that, since there is no suffering greater than dwelling in a womb. (68)
These many sufferings exist in the world; yet even so, hell is distinguished as superior.
For at the moment of entering the womb, there is indeed the supreme suffering, consisting entirely of excrement, urine, and semen. (69)
I shall indeed go forth into homelessness, O father, for life is certainly not eternal;
agitated by the fear of being destroyed in the womb, I am terrified even of death. (70)
No dharma superior to the householder’s stage of life exists for those dwelling in the forest;
devoted to the worship of their gurus and the gods, they protect all men. (71)
The undertaking of a household is impermanent; the bondage of saṃsāra is suffering.
Alas! The deluded are agitated, for though devoid of qualities, they rely upon qualities.
For those who were born in the forests of Śrī Savātapas and met their death right there,
their merit is very small, as they were ignorant of the enjoyment of desires. (73)
This is a gateway to the monastery wall for binding people through logic, where their youth and wealth are sacrificed. (74)
Many thousands who maintained the vow of lifelong celibacy are seen to have gone to heaven, even without establishing a lineage of offspring. (75)
For it is seen that the other three stages of life arise from the householder;
even the mendicants live [upon his support]. Therefore, the householder’s stage is the most excellent.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity.
Among all four social orders, the householder is indeed preeminent. (77)
Just as all living beings survive by depending on their mother, so do all mendicants subsist by depending on the householder. (78)
For servants always live for the benefit of their master;
indeed, because they are the primary agents, the master enjoys the fruit of that service. (79)
I am the southern direction for both the sun and the firefly.
Drive the chariot of Dharma, not of Adharma; speak truth, not falsehood.
One must not enter into darkness; therefore, wake up, wake up! (101)
Having obtained this human birth, which is as difficult to attain as a flash of lightning, and having reached this supreme state, what other meritorious deed could I have performed? (2)
That all living beings on earth are tormented by physical suffering as well as mental suffering, and yet they continue to breathe— that is truly a marvel.
Even now, I do not see that extent of the earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, bounded by the ocean, which he has enjoyed.
Thousands of Purandaras and hundreds of Cakravartins have been extinguished by time, like lamps by the wind. (5)
Out of greed for union with a beloved, a person is bound by grief;
just as the yak-cow met her death for the sake of her tail at that very same spot.
O Lord, one who is overcome by ignorance, passion, and greed,
and who is assailed by many assemblies, does not go to heaven because of that. (7)
Fie on wealth, which brings about much enmity for men; fie on sovereignty, which is fearful and full of anxieties!
Fie on heaven, where there is the tendency to return once more! And fie, fie on this body, which is the abode of disease! (8)

The seed is the father, the field is the mother-earth, and the rains are the auspicious and inauspicious deeds; Time indeed reaps the living beings who are like the crops in this world, both when they are ripe and when they are unripe.
But at home, having abandoned wealth, and in the cremation ground, having left behind friends and kinsmen, he departs naked-limbed and empty-handed, like one who has been robbed. (10)
One should practice the Dharma while still young, for life is impermanent;
just as ripe fruits are constantly in fear of falling, so too is there constant danger for living beings. (11)
Behold the majesty of the Dharma when it is practiced constantly:
it brings about one's own welfare and becomes dear to the world. (12)
O Goddess, what extremely terrible suffering have I experienced, by which I have been thoroughly smeared for a long time? 13.
The hells, numbering twenty-one according to those devoted to the scriptures,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the suffering near the dwelling in the womb.
Sons born of you have been protected by their sons, and others have been born of yet others; behold this delusion of saṃsāra. (15)
Austerity is my father, and Dharma is my grandfather;
my great-grandfather is the body of Maheśvara, which is the goal attained through the renunciation of even that.
Likewise, in human existence, from birth to birth again and again, there is mutual wandering; but where there is no further birth, O dear one, there is no doubt regarding that state. (17)

In the spring season, amidst the forest interiors thick with clusters of flowers and filled with the essence of nectar between them, that man who does not enjoy the space between her breasts has a life whose end is already destroyed. (18)

That man who, having cast aside other doctrines, does not practice another form of knowledge, another state of liberation, another dharma, another stage of yoga, or another meditation—his life alone is truly lived. (19)
The life of that man who pursues the interior of a woman's mouth—which has its lips adorned with betel-juice and its lower lip scented by the waves of cloves—is lived in vain. (20)
